note: Neither `payload` nor `payloadBase64Url` — a JWS with no payload is not what this task signs, and a custodian that defaulted one would be choosing what the key vouches for.
Both `payload` and `payloadBase64Url` — exactly one is allowed, so the custodian never has to pick which of two payloads the producer meant to sign.
Missing `keyId` — the custodian chooses `alg` from the key, so without one there is nothing to sign with and no algorithm to set.

A top-level `algorithm` member — the producer cannot name the algorithm (keys/sign's shape). `additionalProperties: false` keeps it out; an `alg` inside `header` is refused by the custodian as headerMemberForbidden.

A `signingInput` member carrying raw bytes to sign — the generic oracle's shape. The custodian builds the signing input itself; additionalProperties: false is what keeps this task from becoming keys/sign under another name.
`payload` as a string rather than a JSON object — a non-JSON payload goes in `payloadBase64Url`, so the custodian never guesses whether a string is JSON text or bytes.
`payloadBase64Url` in standard base64 with padding — the pattern refuses `+`, `/` and `=`.
`header` as an array rather than an object — a JOSE header is a JSON object.
Bare/unnamespaced ext key — SPEC §4.5.1 producer rule.
Response without `jws` — the one member the task exists to return.
Response `alg` outside the closed set — `none` is never a value a custodian chooses.
A JWS with an empty signature segment — an unsigned token is not a response to a signing request, and the pattern requires three non-empty segments.
Response smuggling key material beside the JWS — additionalProperties: false on the response is what makes 'never the private key' checkable.
Missing required `subject` — a certificate request names who is to be certified, and a custodian that defaulted one would be choosing the name on the producer's behalf.
Empty `subject` — an empty distinguished name would make the subject alternative name the only identity, which RFC 5280 handles with a critical extension this task never requests.
`subject` as a DN string — the custodian never parses a distinguished name; the structured attribute list is what lets it encode exactly what was asked.
An attribute type outside the closed set (passing an OID through) — each type's encoding is fixed by the specification, so an unknown one cannot be encoded on trust.
A lower-cased attribute short name — these are externally owned names carried verbatim (`CN`, not `cn`).
An attribute with an empty value — X.520 attribute values are never empty.
A multi-valued RDN smuggled as an extra member — each element is one single-valued RDN.
A raw DER CertificationRequestInfo to sign — the generic oracle's shape. additionalProperties: false is what keeps the custodian building the request itself.
A requested extension — extensions come from the CA, and only the subject alternative name is ever requested.
A wildcard dNSName — this task requests exact host names only.
An unknown subjectAltNames kind (`ip`) — the set of kinds is closed.
An empty `subjectAltNames` object — present means at least one name; absent means none.
A URI with a space — uniformResourceIdentifier entries are printable ASCII without spaces.
Bare/unnamespaced ext key — SPEC §4.5.1 producer rule.
Response without `publicKey` — the producer confirms the request is for the key it meant from this member.
A bare base64 DER rather than PEM `CERTIFICATE REQUEST` armour.
Response smuggling key material beside the request — additionalProperties: false on the response is what makes 'never the private key' checkable.
